title: Lab2Sim Turns 218 Experiment Videos Into Interactive Sims
summary: South China University and HK PolyU release Lab2Sim, a benchmark converting 218 science experiment videos into interactive web simulations with 11,881 rubric
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Lab2Sim benchmark packages 218 chemistry, physics and biology experiment videos with 11,881 rubric items evaluating simulation fidelity and operability.
- All eight tested multimodal systems achieved 93% runnable rate, but none exceeded 60% apparatus fidelity without the EduVideo2Code refinement method.
- EduVideo2Code lifts apparatus fidelity by 20-24 points through hierarchical procedure extraction, state machine encoding and execution-based verification loops.


South China University of Technology and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University have released Lab2Sim, a benchmark that converts 218 science experiment videos into interactive web simulations. Officially released on November 3, 2026, the dataset pairs chemistry, physics and biology demonstrations with 11,881 rubric items that evaluate how faithfully generated code reproduces apparatus, procedures and state transitions. Every specification was human-verified against source video in an average of 13 minutes per clip.


## Release Date and Availability


Officially released on November 3, 2026, Lab2Sim packages videos collected from Bilibili and YouTube alongside video-grounded specifications detailing apparatus, ordered steps, preconditions and state transitions. The authors verified each draft specification frame-by-frame, ensuring alignment with the source material. Dataset and code will be available at the project page, joining a narrow set of education-focused AI benchmarks tracked in recent months.


## Benchmark Structure and Evaluation Rubric


The 218 videos span three scientific domains: chemistry, physics and biology. Each video is paired with a specification instantiated into 11,881 rubric items that score four dimensions: Apparatus Fidelity, Procedure Execution, Procedural Constraint Compliance and a binary Runnable Rate flag. Human reviewers scored each generated page by executing it in a browser and comparing apparatus rendering, step sequencing and interactive behavior against the video ground truth. The paper frames the evaluation plainly: a high runnable rate says little about fidelity.


## Baseline Performance Across Eight Systems


Six multimodal systems were tested directly: Seed-2.1-Pro, GLM-5.3-Flash, GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-6-Astra, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Kimi-K3. All eight configurations achieved a runnable rate above 93%, meaning the generated HTML pages loaded and executed in a browser. Yet none of the six direct baselines reached 60% on apparatus fidelity. Scores ranged from 20.62 to 61.32 on Apparatus Fidelity and 20.11 to 41.40 on Procedure Execution. GPT-6-Astra led Procedural Constraint Compliance at 44.83%, but the gap between running code and faithful reproduction remained wide.


## EduVideo2Code Method Lifts Fidelity by 20 to 24 Points


The authors introduced EduVideo2Code, a compile-verify-repair pipeline that extracts procedures hierarchically from video, encodes them as explicit state machines, then executes the generated page and attempts repairs until a score threshold is met. On GLM-5.3-Flash, the method lifted apparatus fidelity by 20.88 points; on GPT-5.6-Sol, by 24.15 points. Runnable Rate reached 100% on both backbones. Procedural Constraint Compliance gains varied sharply: 22.00 points on GLM-5.3-Flash versus only 1.19 on GPT-5.6-Sol, suggesting backbone-specific sensitivities to state-machine refinement.


- Apparatus Fidelity gains: 20.88 points (GLM-5.3-Flash), 24.15 points (GPT-5.6-Sol)
- Runnable Rate: 100% on both tested backbones
- Procedural Constraint Compliance: 22.00 points (GLM) vs. 1.19 points (GPT)


## Remaining Gaps in Subtle Physics Rendering


Even with EduVideo2Code, the benchmark exposes limits in visual fidelity. One case study highlighted condensation on a beaker wall conveyed through text rather than a corresponding visual change in the simulation. The authors note that subtle physics phenomena, transient state changes and fine-grained apparatus details remain difficult for current multimodal models to capture and translate into executable code. The gap between a running page and a pedagogically useful simulation persists.


## What This Means


Lab2Sim establishes a new standard for evaluating video-to-code generation in educational contexts. The benchmark demonstrates that high runnable rates mask significant fidelity shortfalls, and that explicit state-machine representations paired with execution-based repair loops can close part of that gap. For educators and edtech developers, the work points toward a future where instructional videos can be semi-automatically converted into interactive labs, though human oversight will remain necessary to verify subtle physics and apparatus behavior.
